text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":48778,"ns":0,"title":"Action theory (philosophy)","extract":"Action theory or theory of action is an area in philosophy concerned with theories about the processes causing willful human bodily movements of a more or less complex kind. title: English Wikipedia article: Ad hoc hypothesis
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":725226,"ns":0,"title":"Ad hoc hypothesis","extract":"In science and philosophy, an ad hoc hypothesis is a hypothesis added to a theory in order to save it from being falsified.\nFor example, a person that wants to believe in leprechauns can avoid ever being proven wrong by using ad hoc hypotheses (e.g., by adding \"they are invisible\", then \"their motives are complex\", and so on).","description":"Addition to a theory to prevent falsification","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Correspondence theory of truth
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":505176,"ns":0,"title":"Correspondence theory of truth","extract":"In metaphysics and philosophy of language, the correspondence theory of truth states that the truth or falsity of a statement is determined only by how it relates to the world and whether it accurately describes (i.e., corresponds with) that world. \nCorrespondence theories claim that true beliefs and true statements correspond to the actual state of affairs.","description":"Theory that truth means correspondence with reality","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Availability cascade
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":19887527,"ns":0,"title":"Availability cascade","extract":"An availability cascade is a self-reinforcing cycle that explains the development of certain kinds of collective beliefs. title: English Wikipedia article: Critical thinking
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":276872,"ns":0,"title":"Critical thinking","extract":"Critical thinking is the process of analyzing available facts, evidence, observations, and arguments to reach sound conclusions or informed choices. text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":1655450,"ns":0,"title":"Informal fallacy","extract":"Informal fallacies are a type of incorrect argument in natural language. text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":3637937,"ns":0,"title":"Formal fallacy","extract":"In logic and philosophy, a formal fallacy is a pattern of reasoning with a flaw in its logical structure (the logical relationship between the premises and the conclusion). title: English Wikipedia article: Skepticism
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":26810,"ns":0,"title":"Skepticism","extract":"Skepticism (US) or scepticism (UK) is a questioning attitude or doubt toward knowledge claims that are seen as mere belief or dogma. text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":70661484,"ns":0,"title":"Action bias","extract":"Action bias is the psychological phenomenon where people tend to favor action over inaction, even when there is no indication that doing so would point towards a better result. text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":304939,"ns":0,"title":"Philosophical logic","extract":"Understood in a narrow sense, philosophical logic is the area of logic that studies the application of logical methods to philosophical problems, often in the form of extended logical systems like modal logic. text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":13464156,"ns":0,"title":"Adverse inference","extract":"Adverse inference is a legal inference, adverse to the concerned party, drawn from silence or absence of requested evidence. title: English Wikipedia article: Candle problem
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":25821227,"ns":0,"title":"Candle problem","extract":"The candle problem or candle task, also known as Duncker's candle problem, is a cognitive performance test, measuring the influence of functional fixedness on a participant's problem solving capabilities. text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":21771273,"ns":0,"title":"Alvin Plantinga's free-will defense","extract":"Alvin Plantinga's free-will defense is a logical argument developed by the American analytic philosopher Alvin Plantinga and published in its final version in his 1977 book God, Freedom, and Evil. text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":3697482,"ns":0,"title":"A series and B series","extract":"In metaphysics, the A series and the B series are two different descriptions of the temporal ordering relation among events. text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":47278,"ns":0,"title":"Cognitive bias","extract":"A cognitive bias is a systematic pattern of deviation from the norm or rationality in judgment. title: English Wikipedia article: Pseudoscience
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":23047,"ns":0,"title":"Pseudoscience","extract":"Pseudoscience consists of statements, beliefs, or practices that claim to be scientific but are inherently incompatible with the scientific method. title: English Wikipedia article: A priori and a posteriori
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":6679056,"ns":0,"title":"A priori and a posteriori","extract":"In epistemology, a priori (‘from the earlier’) and a posteriori (‘from the later’) are the two categories of knowledge, justification, or argument, determining whether or not a proposition is reliant on outside sensory experience. text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":1802769,"ns":0,"title":"History and philosophy of science","extract":"The history and philosophy of science (HPS) is an academic discipline that encompasses the history of science and the philosophy of science. title: English Wikipedia article: B-theory of time
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":10188326,"ns":0,"title":"B-theory of time","extract":"The B-theory of time, also called the tenseless theory of time, is one of two positions regarding the temporal ordering of events in the philosophy of time. title: English Wikipedia article: Deflationary theory of truth
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":601131,"ns":0,"title":"Deflationary theory of truth","extract":"In philosophy and logic, a deflationary theory of truth (also semantic deflationism or simply deflationism) is one of a family of theories that all have in common the claim that assertions of predicate truth of a statement do not attribute a property called \"truth\" to such a statement.","description":"Family of philosophical theories","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Archival research
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":25351850,"ns":0,"title":"Archival research","extract":"Archival research is a type of research which involves seeking out and extracting evidence from archival records. title: English Wikipedia article: Agent causation
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":52363072,"ns":0,"title":"Agent causation","extract":"Agent causation (or agent causality) is a category of determination in metaphysics, where a being who is not an event—namely an agent—can cause events (particularly the agent's own actions). title: English Wikipedia article: Adaptive reasoning
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":21196956,"ns":0,"title":"Adaptive reasoning","extract":"Adaptive reasoning refers to a problem solving strategy that adapts thinking to address a problem as it changes and evolves.","description":"Problem solving strategy","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

text:
{"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":675,"ns":0,"title":"Affirming the consequent","extract":"In propositional logic, affirming the consequent (also known as converse error, fallacy of the converse, or confusion of necessity and sufficiency) is a formal fallacy (or an invalid form of argument) that is committed when, in the context of an indicative conditional statement, it is stated that because the consequent is true, therefore the antecedent is true. It takes on the following form:

If P, then Q.
Q.
Therefore, P.
which may also be phrased as

  
    
      
        P
        →
        Q
      
    
    {\displaystyle P\rightarrow Q}
  
    (P implies Q)

  
    
      
        ∴
        Q
        →
        P
      
    
    {\displaystyle \therefore Q\rightarrow P}
  
    (therefore, Q implies P)
For example, it may be true that a broken lamp would cause a room to become dark.","description":"Type of fallacious argument (logical fallacy)","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Empiric school
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":20517233,"ns":0,"title":"Empiric school","extract":"The Empiric school of medicine (Empirics, Empiricists, or Empirici, Greek: Ἐμπειρικοί) was a school of medicine founded in Alexandria the middle of the third century BC. The school was a major influence on ancient Greek and Roman medicine. The school's name is derived from the word empeiria (ἐμπειρία \"experience\") because they professed to derive their knowledge from experiences only, and in doing so set themselves in opposition to the Dogmatic school.","description":"School of medicine in ancient Greece and Rome","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Cartesianism
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":13291712,"ns":0,"title":"Cartesianism","extract":"Cartesianism is the philosophical and scientific system of René Descartes and its subsequent development by other seventeenth century thinkers, most notably François Poullain de la Barre, Nicolas Malebranche and Baruch Spinoza. Descartes is often regarded as the first thinker to emphasize the use of reason to develop the natural sciences.","description":"Philosophical and scientific system of René Descartes","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Accident (philosophy)
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":741128,"ns":0,"title":"Accident (philosophy)","extract":"An accident (Greek συμβεβηκός), in metaphysics and philosophy, is a property that the entity or substance has contingently, without which the substance can still retain its identity. An accident does not affect its essence, according to many philosophers.","description":"Philosophical attribute","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Agentive logic
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":81741865,"ns":0,"title":"Agentive logic","extract":"Agentive logic (also called the logic of action or logic of agency) is the field of philosophical logic and logic in computer science that studies formal representations of agents, their actions, and their abilities. An agentive logic in the narrower sense is a formal system whose primitive operators express that an agent does something, can do something, or sees to it that something is the case.","description":"Field of philosophical and mathematical logic studying agency and action","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Catch-22 (logic)
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":1172067,"ns":0,"title":"Catch-22 (logic)","extract":"A catch-22 is a paradoxical situation from which an individual cannot escape because of contradictory rules or limitations. title: English Wikipedia article: Arbitrary inference
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":18550051,"ns":0,"title":"Arbitrary inference","extract":"Arbitrary inference is a classic tenet of cognitive therapy created by Aaron T. title: English Wikipedia article: Analogy
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":103533,"ns":0,"title":"Analogy","extract":"Analogy is a comparison or correspondence between two things (or two groups of things) because of a third element that they are considered to share.\nLogically, it is an inference or an argument from one particular to another particular, as opposed to deduction, induction, and abduction.","description":"Form of figurative language","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Absolute (philosophy)
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":21350938,"ns":0,"title":"Absolute (philosophy)","extract":"In philosophy (often specifically metaphysics), the absolute, in most common usage, is an absolute perfect, self-sufficient reality that depends upon nothing external to itself. title: English Wikipedia article: Cognitive justice
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":30384825,"ns":0,"title":"Cognitive justice","extract":"The concept of cognitive justice is based on the recognition of the plurality of knowledge and expresses the right of the different forms of knowledge to co-exist. \nIndian scholar Shiv Visvanathan coined the term cognitive justice in his 1997 book \"A Carnival for Science: Essays on science, technology and development\".","description":"Decolonial theory","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Admissible heuristic
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":11338826,"ns":0,"title":"Admissible heuristic","extract":"In computer science, specifically in algorithms related to pathfinding, a heuristic function is said to be admissible if it never overestimates the cost of reaching the goal, i.e. the cost it estimates to reach the goal is not higher than the lowest possible cost from the current point in the path.","description":"Computer science pathfinding concept","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Alphabet of human thought
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":722152,"ns":0,"title":"Alphabet of human thought","extract":"The alphabet of human thought (Latin: alphabetum cogitationum humanarum) is a concept originally proposed by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz that provides a universal way to represent and analyze ideas and relationships by breaking down their component pieces. title: English Wikipedia article: Abductive reasoning
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":60459,"ns":0,"title":"Abductive reasoning","extract":"Abductive reasoning (also called abduction, abductive inference, or retroduction) is a form of logical inference that seeks the simplest and most likely conclusion from a set of observations. title: English Wikipedia article: Actor–network theory
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":505093,"ns":0,"title":"Actor–network theory","extract":"Actor–network theory (ANT) is a theoretical and methodological approach to social theory where everything in the social and natural worlds exists in constantly shifting networks of relationships. title: English Wikipedia article: Argument from analogy
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":33404319,"ns":0,"title":"Argument from analogy","extract":"Argument from analogy is a special type of inductive argument, where perceived similarities are used as a basis to infer some further similarity that has not been observed yet. title: English Wikipedia article: Ad personam
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":78131919,"ns":0,"title":"Ad personam","extract":"In an argument, ad personam, short for argumentum ad personam, is a tactic aimed at discrediting one's opponent by attacking their personality, unrelated to the substance of the debate.","description":"Attacking an opponent's inherent identity rather than their arguments","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Denying the antecedent
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":144793,"ns":0,"title":"Denying the antecedent","extract":"Denying the antecedent (also known as denial of the antecedent, inverse error, or fallacy of the inverse) is a formal fallacy of inferring the inverse from an original statement. title: English Wikipedia article: Antipedagogy
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":75723480,"ns":0,"title":"Antipedagogy","extract":"Antipedagogy (German: Antipädagogik; Ancient Greek: anti-against + pais-child, boy + agein- lead; UK: ), sometimes spelled anti-pedagogy with the hyphen, is a critical theory that examines traditional pedagogical dynamics, particularly scrutinizing the exercise of parental or educational authority as a violation of human rights. title: English Wikipedia article: Antinomy
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":3175,"ns":0,"title":"Antinomy","extract":"In philosophy, an antinomy (; Ancient Greek: antí 'against' + nómos 'law') is a real or apparent contradiction between two conclusions, both of which seem justified. title: English Wikipedia article: Communicative rationality
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":2463551,"ns":0,"title":"Communicative rationality","extract":"Communicative rationality or communicative reason (German: kommunikative Rationalität) is a theory or set of theories which describes human rationality as a necessary outcome of successful communication. title: English Wikipedia article: Analogy of the divided line
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":31068,"ns":0,"title":"Analogy of the divided line","extract":"The analogy of the divided line (Ancient Greek: γραμμὴ δίχα τετμημένη, romanized: grammē dicha tetmēmenē) is presented by the Greek philosopher Plato in the Republic (509d–511e). title: English Wikipedia article: AI trust paradox
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":78010004,"ns":0,"title":"AI trust paradox","extract":"The AI trust paradox (also known as the verisimilitude paradox) is the phenomenon where advanced artificial intelligence models become so proficient at mimicking human-like language and behavior that users increasingly struggle to determine if the information generated is accurate or simply plausible.\nUnlike earlier concerns such as Moravec's paradox, which highlighted the surprising difficulty in replicating simple human functions in AI, and the automation paradox, which deals with balancing automation and human control, the AI trust paradox specifically addresses the issue of verisimilitude—the appearance of truth that leads to misplaced trust.","description":"Artificial intelligence models","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Absolute space and time
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":862898,"ns":0,"title":"Absolute space and time","extract":"Absolute space and time is a concept in physics and philosophy about the properties of the universe. title: English Wikipedia article: Effective theory
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":2914954,"ns":0,"title":"Effective theory","extract":"In science, an effective theory is a deliberately limited  scientific theory applicable under specific circumstances. In practice, all theories are effective theories, with the name \"effective theory\" being used to signal that the limitations are built in by design.","description":"Type of approximation to an underlying physical theory","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Affect heuristic
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":3044780,"ns":0,"title":"Affect heuristic","extract":"The affect heuristic is a  heuristic, a mental shortcut that allows people to make decisions and solve problems quickly and efficiently, in which current emotion—fear, pleasure, surprise, etc.—influences decisions. text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":25390717,"ns":0,"title":"Academic skepticism","extract":"Academic skepticism was the philosophy of the skeptical period of the Academy dating from around 266 BC, when Arcesilaus became scholarch, until around 90 BC, when Antiochus of Ascalon rejected skepticism, although individual philosophers, such as Favorinus and his teacher Plutarch, continued to defend skepticism after this date. text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":2972,"ns":0,"title":"Abstraction","extract":"Abstraction is the process of generalizing rules and concepts from specific examples, literal (real or concrete) signifiers, first principles, or other methods. title: English Wikipedia article: Black swan theory
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":7361848,"ns":0,"title":"Black swan theory","extract":"The black swan theory or theory of black swan events is a metaphor that describes an event that comes as a surprise, has a major effect, and is often inappropriately rationalized after the fact with the benefit of hindsight. text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":2143899,"ns":0,"title":"Closed circle","extract":"A closed-circle argument is one that is unfalsifiable.\nPsychoanalytic theory, for example, is held up by the proponents of Karl Popper as an of an ideology rather than a science.","description":"Unfalsifiable argument","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":1003483,"ns":0,"title":"Epistemic theories of truth","extract":"In philosophy and epistemology, epistemic theories of truth are attempts to analyze the notion of truth in terms of epistemic notions such as knowledge, belief, acceptance, verification, justification, and perspective. \nA variety of such conceptions can be classified into verificationist theories, perspectivist or relativist theories, and pragmatic theories.","description":"Attempts to analyze the concept of truth","descriptionsource":"local"}]}}

title: English Wikipedia article: Blinded experiment
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":277248,"ns":0,"title":"Blinded experiment","extract":"In a blind or blinded experiment, information that could influence participants or investigators is withheld until the experiment is completed. title: English Wikipedia article: Dispersed knowledge
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":221284,"ns":0,"title":"Dispersed knowledge","extract":"Dispersed knowledge in economics is the notion that no single agent has information as to all of the factors which influence prices and production throughout the system. title: English Wikipedia article: Belief revision
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":1187311,"ns":0,"title":"Belief revision","extract":"Belief revision (also called belief change) is the process of changing beliefs to take into account a new piece of information. title: English Wikipedia article: Analytic reasoning
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":5163440,"ns":0,"title":"Analytic reasoning","extract":"Analytical reasoning, also known as analytical thinking, refers to the ability to look at information, be it qualitative or quantitative in nature, and discern patterns within the information. title: English Wikipedia article: Backward induction
text: {"batchcomplete":true,"query":{"pages":[{"pageid":2060912,"ns":0,"title":"Backward induction","extract":"Backward induction is the process of determining a sequence of optimal choices by reasoning from the endpoint of a problem or situation back to its beginning using individual events or actions.
